_about: Field guide cards shown with each hotspot layer. Written from the sources listed per card (researched 2026-10-23). Not legal advice: the land manager has the final word.

general.title: Before any trip
points: Check the legal colour of the exact spot on the map, then confirm with the land manager. Green is not a guarantee: closures, claims and local rules change.
Hand tools only on public land. Personal use only; selling or trading needs a permit or contract (BLM, Forest Service).
Never collect vertebrate fossils (bones, teeth, fish) or artifacts (arrowheads, old bottles) on public land.
Mining claims: the claimant holds the minerals. Ask before collecting on a claim (orange on the map).
Tell someone your plan; many of these spots are past cell coverage.

agate_jasper.title: Agate, jasper & chalcedony
agate_jasper.what: All are chalcedony (microcrystalline quartz). Agate is translucent and often banded; jasper is opaque because of impurities. Both break with smooth, shell-like (conchoidal) fractures and are hard enough that a knife won't scratch them.
identify: Backlight test: hold a stone up to the sun or a flashlight. Light glowing through it, even foggily, means agate; fully opaque means jasper or another rock.
Wet the stones (spray bottle) to bring out colour and banding.
Colour alone doesn't identify them; Ellensburg blue in particular has many pale look-alikes. A true blue stays blue in sunlight, while many pale stones look pinkish when held up to the sun.
where: They form in gas pockets and cracks in volcanic rock, especially basalt flows, then weather out and wash downhill and downstream.
Look on gravel bars, especially fresh ones after spring runoff, in creeks draining basalt or volcanic country, and on eroding slopes below agate-bearing flows.
Ellensburg blue: Teanaway Basalt country north of Ellensburg (Reecer Creek, Green Canyon, Thorp toward Cle Elum). Mostly private land; Rock N Tomahawk Ranch charges a small fee.
Red Top Mountain (Wenatchee National Forest, off Hwy 97 at Blewett Pass) has agate and geode beds on public land.
how: Walk slowly with the sun behind you so translucent stones light up; low morning or evening sun is best.
Focus on the upstream heads of gravel bars and the lines where coarse gravel collects.
Late summer and fall low water exposes the most gravel.

geode_thunderegg.title: Geodes & thundereggs
geode_thunderegg.what: Thundereggs are solid nodules with a lumpy rhyolite shell and an agate, jasper or opal core; they form in rhyolitic ash and flows. Geodes are hollow and often crystal-lined; in this region they come from gas pockets in volcanic rock (e.g. Red Top's quartz and calcite geodes).
identify: Thundereggs are round to knobby and feel heavy and solid for their size; hollow geodes feel lighter.
Weathered eggs can look like ordinary round rocks: the round shape itself is the clue.
Look-alikes include concretions and iron nodules.
where: Rhyolite, tuff and volcanic-ash beds (felsic volcanic on this map), and the gullies and streambeds below them where the soft ash has eroded away.
Basalt and andesite flows with gas pockets for geodes.
how: Scan eroding ash slopes and the washes below them for round lumps.
When digging one out of the ash, mark which way was up; it helps decide where to cut later.
geode_thunderegg.model_note: Few reported finds in this region, so this layer is a rule-based geology score (rhyolite/tuff and vesicular volcanic rock), not a trained prediction.

quartz_crystal.title: Quartz crystals & amethyst
quartz_crystal.what: Six-sided quartz points, clear (rock crystal), smoky or purple (amethyst). They grow in open spaces: pegmatite pockets in granite, hydrothermal veins and volcanic cavities.
identify: A steel knife won't scratch quartz.
Real amethyst is usually deepest purple at the crystal tips and fades toward the base; glass and dyed fakes have flat, even colour.
where: Granite and pegmatite country, especially where the granite has rotted to coarse sand (grus).
Quartz veins along faults; old mine dumps of quartz-vein mines.
Creek beds below crystal-bearing rock collect weathered-out crystals.
how: At a vein, dig around its base for crystals that have weathered out before trying to extract any.
Follow pegmatite zones in decomposed granite; pockets are hit-or-miss and take patience.
Screen creek gravel and soil below productive outcrops.
gear: long flathead screwdriver and needle-nose pliers for pockets
quartz_crystal.model_note: Few reported finds in this region, so this layer is a rule-based geology score (granite/pegmatite, faults, metamorphic rock), not a trained prediction.

petrified_wood.title: Petrified & opalized wood
petrified_wood.what: Wood replaced by silica (quartz, chalcedony or opal). In central Washington, basalt lava flows buried forests about 15 million years ago, which is why the region has so much.
identify: Look for wood grain, growth rings, knots or a log-like shape in something rock-hard and heavy.
A knife blade won't scratch it.
Opalized wood often looks waxy or glassy and is somewhat softer than quartzy wood.
where: Sedimentary layers between basalt flows (e.g. the Ellensburg and Latah formations) and the slopes and washes below them.
Saddle Mountains east of Mattawa (BLM, west end recommended; reportedly no collecting in sections 7, 11 and 13; private land mixed in on the east end).
NOT inside Ginkgo Petrified Forest State Park at Vantage: no collecting.
how: Walk washes and hillsides scanning for the wood-grain texture; fragments on the surface point uphill to the source layer.
BLM limit: 25 lb plus one piece per day, 250 lb per year, personal use only.

fossils.title: Fossils (plants & invertebrates)
fossils.what: Leaf, insect, shell and other invertebrate fossils in sedimentary rock. The region's stars are the Eocene lake beds at Republic (Stonerose) and the Miocene Clarkia/Latah lake beds, where leaves can keep their original fall colours.
identify: Leaf impressions show veins and edges on split surfaces of shale or mudstone.
Shells show regular ribs or symmetric outlines in limestone and sandstone.
where: Fine-grained sedimentary rock: shale, mudstone, lake beds and limestone, at outcrops, road cuts and old spoil piles.
Fee sites are the easy start: Stonerose (Republic), Clarkia Fossil Bowl and Huckleberry Garnet Mine (Clarkia area).
how: Shale splits along its bedding layers: work along them with a knife or chisel (at Clarkia a dull butter knife works).
There's no reliable way to tell from outside which slab holds a fossil; split lots of them. Check the loose debris below an outcrop first for signs.
Older, dried-out piles often split better than fresh wet rock.
gear: newspaper or toilet paper and bags for wrapping
fossils.legal: Vertebrate fossils (bones, teeth, fish) are off-limits on US public land; common invertebrate and plant fossils are OK in reasonable personal amounts on BLM land. Alberta: fossils may NOT leave the province without a permit. BC: small amounts of common fossils by hand; you're a caretaker, and selling is banned.

opal.title: Opal
opal.what: Hydrated silica: common opal (no flashes of colour) is far more common than precious or fire opal. In this region it fills cavities in basalt and rhyolite and replaces wood.
identify: Waxy to glassy look, softer than quartz; precious opal shows flashes of colour (play-of-colour).
where: Gas cavities and seams in basalt (Mondovi, Lincoln County, is a known precious-opal locality) and rhyolite; opalized wood in central Washington basin sediments.
Klinker opal claim near Vernon, BC: fee digging in season (verify current status).
how: Break open vesicular basalt near known spots and look for seams and fillings; check talus below cavity-rich flows.
opal.model_note: Few reported finds in this region, so this layer is a rule-based geology score, not a trained prediction.

garnet.title: Garnet
garnet.what: Hard, glassy, usually dark red to purple-red crystals, often ball-shaped with many faces. North Idaho's Emerald Creek almandine garnets can show a four- or six-rayed star.
identify: Dark red, glassy and harder than most rocks; crystals look like little multi-faceted balls.
Being heavy and hard, they concentrate in stream gravels with other heavy minerals (magnetite, ilmenite, zircon).
where: Metamorphic rock: schist, gneiss and amphibolite (metamorphic on this map), especially where it has weathered.
Creek gravels and dark sands downstream of garnet-bearing schist.
how: Screen creek gravel and pan the dark sand.

Emerald Creek Garnet Area (Forest Service, timed tickets) is CLOSED for the rest of 2026 because its dug supply ran out; Huckleberry Garnet Mine nearby is the private alternative ($5 + $40/lb in 2026).

pegmatite_gems.title: Pegmatite & metamorphic gems
pegmatite_gems.what: Beryl (including aquamarine), tourmaline, topaz, zircon, corundum and sapphire, kyanite and staurolite. Most grow in pegmatites (very coarse granite) or high-grade metamorphic rock.
identify: Beryl: six-sided, often pale green-blue prisms. Tourmaline: striated, often black (schorl) prisms with a triangular cross-section. Kyanite: blue bladed crystals. Staurolite: brown crosses ('fairy crosses').
where: Pegmatite dikes and coarse granite (granitic on this map); schist and gneiss for kyanite, staurolite and garnet.
Mine dumps of old pegmatite prospects in the USGS and BC mineral records.
how: Look for unusually coarse-grained light-coloured rock (pegmatite) in granite country and check its edges and pockets.
Check claim status before working any old prospect.

copper_minerals.title: Malachite, azurite & chrysocolla
copper_minerals.what: Bright green (malachite), deep blue (azurite) and blue-green (chrysocolla) copper minerals that form where copper ore weathers near the surface.
identify: Vivid green or blue crusts, stains and nodules on rock from old copper workings.
where: Dumps of old copper prospects and mines (from the USGS and BC mineral records), many in the BC and NE Washington mining districts.
how: Collect from the dump piles, never inside workings: the old miners already broke the rock out for you.
Check claim status first; many old mines are on active claims or private patented land.
safety: Never enter shafts, adits or pits: hidden vertical openings, collapsing edges and bad air kill people every year.
Copper minerals make toxic dust when broken: wear a dust mask, wash your hands, and don't eat on site. Some old sites also have arsenic in the soil.
Stay back from pit edges and steep dump faces.

uv_minerals.title: Fluorescent minerals (UV night hunting)
uv_minerals.what: Some minerals glow under ultraviolet light. Scheelite (a tungsten ore) glows bright bluish-white under shortwave UV; fluorite and hyalite opal glow too. This region has hundreds of old tungsten and fluorite prospects.
identify: Scheelite: bright blue-white glow under shortwave (about 255 nm) LED UV; the colour can look different with an old mercury-tube lamp. Powellite, a common companion, glows yellow instead.
where: Dumps of old tungsten (scheelite) and fluorite prospects, often in contact zones between granite and limestone (skarn).
how: Go after dark (or into deep shade) on a moonless night; scout the dump by daylight first so you know the footing.
Sweep the lamp low over dump rock and look for the glow.
safety: Shortwave UV can burn eyes and skin: wear UV-blocking glasses and never look into the lamp.
Mine-dump hazards apply (see malachite card): no shafts or adits.

placer_gold.title: Placer gold (panning)
placer_gold.what: Gold flakes and occasional small nuggets eroded from veins and concentrated in stream gravels because gold is so heavy.
identify: Real gold stays bright yellow in shade and from every angle and is soft (dents with a pin). Mica and pyrite ('fool's gold') glitter only at certain angles or are brassy and brittle.
where: Inside bends where water slows, the downstream side of boulders, cracks in bedrock, slow water below rapids, and the upstream heads of gravel bars.
Streams in historic placer districts (the USGS and BC records drive this layer).
how: Dig down toward bedrock; gold sinks. Clean out bedrock cracks with small tools.
Busy, well-known spots have been worked for over a century, so try less obvious corners.
placer_gold.legal: Washington: follow WDFW's free 'Gold and Fish' pamphlet (it acts as your permit for hand panning; work windows protect fish spawning and vary by stream; no motorized equipment or dredges). Get landowner permission and check for mining claims everywhere.

lode_gold.title: Lode gold (gold in quartz veins)
lode_gold.what: Gold still in the rock it formed in: specks and wires in white quartz veins, often with pyrite and rusty iron stains. Visible gold is rare; most of it was what the miners took away.
identify: Gold is soft (about 2.5-3): it dents with a pin and never crumbles. Pyrite is hard (6-6.5) and a knife point crumbles it to greenish-black powder.
Gold stays bright from every angle and never tarnishes; pyrite and chalcopyrite look darker in shade.
Rusty, pyrite-rich quartz can carry gold you can't see: only an assay can tell.
where: Old lode-mine dumps and quartz veins in the mining districts (the mine records drive this layer).
Rusty quartz float in creeks below known veins.
how: Break open rusty, cavity-rich (vuggy) quartz and check with a hand lens in sunlight.
Crush and pan a sample of weathered vein material to see if it sheds gold.
safety: Never enter mine tunnels or go near shafts; stay off steep dump faces.
Old mine waste can hold lead and arsenic: gloves, wash hands and finds, no eating on the pile.

lead_zinc_silver.title: Galena, sphalerite & silver ores
lead_zinc_silver.what: The ore minerals of the region's big mining districts (the Coeur d'Alene silver belt, NE Washington): lead-grey galena cubes, resinous sphalerite, and silver minerals like tetrahedrite.
identify: Galena: shiny lead-grey, breaks into perfect cubes, startlingly heavy.
Sphalerite: resinous yellow, brown or black, with a pale yellow-brown streak even from black pieces.
Tetrahedrite: steel-grey metallic, brittle, often in triangular pyramid crystals.
where: Dumps of old lead-zinc-silver mines and prospects (the mine records drive this layer).
how: Look for heavy, metallic pieces on dumps; galena cubes weather out of quartz and carbonate gangue.
safety: Galena and cerussite are lead minerals: never lick or grind them, wash hands, keep away from kids and pets.
The Silver Valley (Bunker Hill) is a contamination zone: don't collect there.
Never enter mine tunnels or go near shafts; stay off steep dump faces.
Old mine waste can hold lead and arsenic: gloves, wash hands and finds, no eating on the pile.

calcite_barite.title: Calcite & barite crystals
calcite_barite.what: Common but often beautiful vein minerals: calcite rhombs and 'dogtooth' points, and heavy tabular barite blades and roses.
identify: Calcite: hardness 3, breaks into slanted rhombs, fizzes readily in a drop of acid.
Barite: hardness 3-3.5, feels far too heavy for a light-coloured mineral (specific gravity ~4.5).
Calcite often fluoresces under UV in many colours.
where: Vein and cavity linings at old mines and in limestone and marble; basalt gas pockets for calcite.
how: Look in cavities on dumps and in quarry faces; check calcite with a UV light at night.
safety: Never enter mine tunnels or go near shafts; stay off steep dump faces.
Old mine waste can hold lead and arsenic: gloves, wash hands and finds, no eating on the pile.

iron_minerals.title: Magnetite & specular hematite
iron_minerals.what: Black, metallic iron oxides: magnetite (strongly magnetic, often in eight-sided crystals) and specular hematite (glittering steel-grey flakes).
identify: Streak tells them apart: hematite always streaks reddish-brown, even when it looks black; magnetite streaks black.
Magnetite is the only common strongly magnetic mineral; some hematite is weakly magnetic because of mixed-in magnetite, so check the streak too.
where: Skarns and iron prospects near granite contacts; black sand in creek gravels (magnetite).
how: Carry a magnet: run it through creek sand or over dump material.

molybdenite.title: Molybdenite
molybdenite.what: Soft, lead-grey metallic flakes and hexagonal tablets, usually in quartz veins in or near granite.
identify: Marks paper like pencil lead (bluish grey); thin flakes bend; greasy feel.
Tells apart from graphite by its bluish tint and setting (granite veins, not schist or marble).
where: Quartz veins and pegmatites in granitic rock, and the skarns around them (the mine records drive this layer).
how: Split quartz vein pieces along fractures: flakes show as silvery hexagons.

epidote.title: Epidote
epidote.what: Pistachio-green prismatic crystals and crusts, common where granite has baked limestone (skarn) and in altered volcanic and metamorphic rock.
identify: Yellowish to pistachio green, glassy, hard (6-7), striated prisms.
Lighter, yellower green than chlorite, which is darker and soft.
where: Skarns at granite-limestone contacts, altered volcanic rock, gneiss and schist.
how: Check fractures and cavities in green-stained rock on dumps and road cuts.

staurolite_kyanite.title: Staurolite & kyanite (fairy crosses)
staurolite_kyanite.what: Metamorphic crystals in schist: brown staurolite, which twins into crosses ('fairy crosses'), and blue blade-shaped kyanite.
identify: Staurolite: brown, six-sided prisms, often crossing at 90° (Roman/Maltese cross) or 60° (St Andrew's cross).
Kyanite: blue-grey blades whose hardness differs along and across the blade.
Host rock: silvery, flaky mica schist.
where: Mica schist country; in North Idaho crosses are panned from creek gravels such as Big Carpenter Creek, one drainage north of Emerald Creek.
how: Weathered schist and the creek gravels below it: staurolite is heavier than ordinary gravel and settles deep, like garnet.
staurolite_kyanite.legal: Many North Idaho creeks cross Potlatch timber land: a recreational permit is required there.

serpentine_jade.title: Serpentine & jade
serpentine_jade.what: Green, greasy-looking rock from ultramafic belts: serpentine (soft) and its tough cousin nephrite jade, which forms from serpentinite.
identify: Serpentine: hardness 3-5 (a knife scratches it), lighter in the hand (2.4-2.8).
Nephrite: about 6-6.5, extremely tough (resists a hammer), heavier (2.9-3.1), rings when tapped.
where: Serpentinite belts along major faults; Washington nephrite is tied to the Darrington-Devils Mountain fault zone; noble serpentine near Chewelah (the Wild Turkey claim).
how: Stream gravels below serpentinite are the safest hunting: no rock breaking needed.
safety: Serpentinite can hold chrysotile ASBESTOS: don't break fibrous rock, keep dust down, wear an N95 when disturbing it.

fluorite.title: Fluorite
fluorite.what: Glassy cubes and octahedra in purple, green, yellow or clear, from veins around granite and in limestone.
identify: Hardness about 4: a knife scratches it, but it scratches calcite.
Breaks along four directions into octahedra (diamond shapes).
Often glows blue-violet under longwave UV.
where: Veins at old mines (often with galena, sphalerite and calcite) and granite-limestone contacts.
how: Look for colourful glassy cubes on dumps; hunt at night with a UV light.
safety: Never enter mine tunnels or go near shafts; stay off steep dump faces.
Old mine waste can hold lead and arsenic: gloves, wash hands and finds, no eating on the pile.

zeolites.title: Zeolites (crystals in basalt pockets)
zeolites.what: Delicate white, clear or pink crystals (chabazite, heulandite, stilbite, natrolite...) that line gas pockets in basalt and andesite.
identify: Soft (3.5-5.5) crystals in basalt vesicles: chabazite cubes-like rhombs, heulandite coffin-shaped plates, stilbite sheaves, natrolite needles.
where: Columbia River Basalt road cuts and quarries, e.g. along Highway 193 west of Clarkston (Snake River) and around Rock Island Dam; dam sites like Skookumchuck are closed.
how: Look for basalt with open gas pockets in fresh road cuts and quarry rubble; wrap finds well, they're fragile.
gear: egg cartons or tissue for fragile crystals
zeolites.legal: Road cuts are often state right-of-way: stay off the travel lanes and don't undercut the slope.
